text: Microsoft Defender for Cloud actually ships as two layers, and mixing them up is where most confusion starts. There's a free, always-on posture layer that scores your configuration, and a separate, paid detection layer that watches for real suspicious behavior. Knowing which one you're looking at changes how you should react to it.

A recommendation is free and always running — it's a static statement that a resource's configuration doesn't meet a best practice, nothing more. A security alert is different: it only exists where a paid Defender plan is actively watching that resource type, and it means something specific and suspicious actually happened. When Defender for Cloud can connect related alerts into one plausible attack sequence, it groups them into an incident, so you triage one story instead of five disconnected tiles.

Here's what a real alert carries: a severity, a MITRE ATT&CK tactic tag telling you where it sits in a typical attack chain, the specific resource involved, and which Defender plan raised it. That last field matters more than people expect — if Defender for Servers isn't enabled on that VM, this exact alert simply never fires. You'd only ever see the underlying configuration recommendations.

Turning on behavioral detection is a deliberate step, not something Foundational CSPM gives you automatically. A command like az security pricing create for Virtual Machines at the Standard tier is what actually enables Defender for Servers on a subscription. Until you do that, that resource type can carry plenty of open recommendations and still never raise a single security alert.

In practice: enable Defender plans only for the resource types you actually run in production, since turning everything on has a real cost. Triage the Secure Score dashboard by potential score impact and exposure, not by raw recommendation count — a small-impact finding on an internet-facing, privileged resource can matter more than a bigger number elsewhere. And forward alerts into Microsoft Sentinel or Defender XDR where you can, so cloud signal correlates with identity and endpoint signal instead of living alone.

That's Defender for Cloud's two-layer model: free posture assessment everywhere, paid behavioral detection where you turn it on. Next lesson crosses over to AWS, where Security Hub and GuardDuty split the same two jobs — finding aggregation and threat detection — in a structurally similar but differently-built way.
